paper.title: What comes after de novo? Automated lead optimization of proteins with CRADLE-1
paper.abstract: Lead optimization remains the longest and most expensive step in pre-clinical drug discovery, typically consuming 12-36 months whilst costing $5M-$15M per candidate. We introduce 'CRADLE-1', an automated framework for protein engineering. While CRADLE-1 supports the full process of drug discovery and industrial protein engineering pipelines, including hit identification and de novo binder design, this work focuses on its application to multi-property lead optimization across protein modalities (VHHs, scFvs, IgGs, peptides, enzymes, CRISPR systems, vaccines). We show it is 4-7x faster than rational design, as measured by the number of wet lab rounds required. We provide in-vitro validation across all of the above modalities, typically optimizing multiple properties simultaneously (single and polyspecific binding down to picomolar, activity, thermostability, ...). Technically, CRADLE-1 starts with pre-trained foundation protein language models (PLMs), which are fine-tuned in unsupervised fashion on evolutionary neighborhoods, in supervised fashion using lab-in-the-loop data, and then deployed in a multi-model workflow. Of additional interest, we find that (a) the end-to-end system may be run in automated fashion; (b) wet lab data may be consumed in 'black box' fashion without knowledge of the underlying biochemical mechanisms; (c) structural data may largely be superseded by sequence-function pairs.
paper.tldr: They built an automated protein-engineering system that fine-tunes protein language models in a lab-in-the-loop workflow and show in-vitro validation of simultaneous multi-property optimization across seven protein modalities, achieving 4-7x speed-up over rational design.
paper.why: CRADLE-1 is a landmark-level biotech advance: an automated, end-to-end AI framework for protein lead optimization validated in the wet lab across many modalities (antibodies, enzymes, CRISPR, vaccines), claiming 4-7x fewer experimental rounds than rational design. It hits the same nerve as AlphaFold for this user — general AI with clear, demonstrated biological application — and its finding that sequence-function data can largely supersede structural data is provocative and reusable. Runner-up method papers (vampW, GeneICL) are strong but more incremental.

summary.tldr: CRADLE-1 is an automated, lab-in-the-loop protein engineering framework from Cradle Bio that fine-tunes foundation protein language models to improve multiple properties of existing protein leads, reporting 4-7x fewer wet-lab rounds than rational design across seven protein modalities.
summary.background: Lead optimization—improving an existing candidate's binding, specificity, activity, and stability—is the longest and most expensive step in pre-clinical drug discovery, typically taking 12-36 months and $5M-$15M per candidate. It is hard because several properties must improve simultaneously, wet-lab testing is slow and costly, and rational or structure-based design often fails to predict how these properties are coupled.
summary.approach: The authors (all Cradle Bio employees) built CRADLE-1, a multi-model workflow that starts from pre-trained foundation protein language models, fine-tunes them unsupervised on 'evolutionary neighborhoods' (related sequence families around the lead) and in a supervised manner on lab-in-the-loop assay data, then uses these models to propose variant libraries each design-build-test cycle. The platform also supports hit identification and de novo binder design, but this paper focuses on lead optimization of existing proteins: VHHs, scFvs, IgGs, peptides, enzymes, CRISPR systems, and vaccines, each with in-vitro validation.
findings: Across all seven modalities, CRADLE-1 required 4-7x fewer wet-lab rounds than rational design to reach its multi-property objectives.
Programs typically optimized several properties at once, including single and polyspecific binding improved down to picomolar, plus activity and thermostability.
The full design-build-test loop can run end-to-end in an automated fashion.
Wet-lab assay data could be consumed in 'black box' fashion, without modeling the underlying biochemistry.
Structural information was largely unnecessary; sequence-function pairs alone sufficed.
summary.why: For someone building ML on biological sequences, this is a concrete industrial example of lab-in-the-loop fine-tuning of PLMs on sequence-function data, with assay results feeding back into foundation models each round. It also speaks to a broader question relevant to multiomics: when do sequence-only, black-box models outperform structure-based, mechanism-aware approaches?
summary.limitations: This is an industry preprint (all authors are Cradle Bio employees, not yet peer-reviewed) with no public datasets, sequences, or per-program metrics beyond the headline claims, so results cannot be independently verified. The '4-7x faster' comparison counts wet-lab rounds rather than cost or success rate, and key details such as the exact base models, fine-tuning setup, and how 'evolutionary neighborhoods' are constructed are underspecified.

also.title: Joint Variable Selection for Omic Biomarkers in Time-to-Event Data
also.abstract: The incidence of the vast majority of neurodegenerative, cancer, and metabolic diseases generally increases exponentially with age. In large-scale biobanks, linking time-to-diagnosis information in electronic health records to multiple genomic (``multiomics'') measures has the potential to reveal the genes and biological pathways involved in the disease onset and progression. To date, association testing has commonly been conducted by testing one variable at a time using semiparametric Cox proportional hazards (CoxPH) models, which ignores correlation structure and increases the risk of false discoveries. To address these issues, we introduce a novel fully parametric Bayesian computational method, vampW, based on the Vector Approximate Message Passing framework applied to a Weibull model. vampW jointly models correlated features, while providing an interpretable hazard structure, producing a continuous survival curve, and incorporating prior knowledge. In an extensive simulation study, we demonstrate that joint modeling of omics data and time-to-event outcomes with vampW, substantially reduces false discoveries in comparison to marginal testing and other forms of joint CoxPH models. In 53,018 individuals from the UK Biobank, vampW identifies 219 protein associations with 24 disease outcomes, most of which are not among the top marginal discoveries. We further correct protein levels for exponential age effects, identifying 1,308 associations and highlighting the sensitivity of the analysis to age-correction methodology. Our findings replicate in independent cohorts using different measurement technologies, within data from Iceland and a novel Generation Scotland proteomics dataset. vampW also achieves significant improvement in the prediction of disease onset times: across 14 outcomes, it reduces the root mean squared error by over 30% and 26%, when compared to CoxPH variants and the deep learning approach DeepSurv, respectively, while maintaining predictive utility in minority populations. In summary, vampW offers accurate and interpretable variable selection and out-of-sample prediction within a single computational framework, making it a powerful tool for dissecting the genomic architecture of common complex disease onset.

also.title: GeneICL: A Tabular Foundation Model for Bulk Transcriptomics
also.abstract: Gene expression is widely measured in biomedicine, yet clinical outcome prediction remains challenging due to high dimensionality, strong feature correlations, and limited labeled data. Large self-supervised transcriptomic foundation models often fail to outperform simple supervised baselines. Tabular foundation models offer an alternative through in-context learning, but are typically pretrained on generic synthetic data rather than transcriptomic structure. We ask whether transcriptomics-aware pretraining, rather than scale, is the missing ingredient. Towards this end, we introduce GeneICL, a 4.2M-parameter tabular foundation model combining a semi-synthetic pretraining prior built from measured bulk expression profiles with a parameter-efficient recurrent architecture. We further enable right-censored survival prediction via a training-free reduction to regression using Cox partial-likelihood residuals. We evaluate GeneICL on 80 clinical outcome-prediction tasks spanning classification, regression, and survival. Tabular foundation models consistently outperform self-supervised transcriptomic models, while GeneICL achieves the best overall rank among evaluated foundation models and tuned baselines. GeneICL does so with up to 387$\times$ fewer parameters, no gradient updates at inference, and predictions within seconds on a laptop CPU.

summary.tldr: GeneICL is a 4.2M-parameter tabular in-context-learning foundation model for bulk RNA-seq that, via a semi-synthetic pretraining prior built from ~548k real expression profiles, achieves the best overall rank across 80 clinical prediction tasks while running in seconds on a laptop CPU.
summary.background: Predicting clinical outcomes from bulk gene expression is a severe n<
summary.approach: The authors build GeneICL, a TabICLv2-derived in-context learner that operates in support-set-fitted PC space (keeping PCs explaining 90% of variance) and replaces the stack of ICL layers with a single weight-tied transformer block applied recurrently (8 steps). Its pretraining prior is semi-synthetic: a VAE trained on 547,829 human ARCHS4 RNA-seq profiles (20,021 genes) generates the covariates, while randomly sampled MLP functions of the PCs supply unlimited classification and regression labels. Right-censored survival is handled training-free by regressing Cox partial-likelihood (null-model martingale) residuals, so one frozen model does classification, regression, and survival with no gradient updates at inference.
findings: On a new benchmark of 80 tasks (27 classification, 25 regression, 28 survival; median cohort sizes 144, 491, and 202.5), tabular foundation models consistently outperform self-supervised transcriptomic models, which trail even tuned baselines like elastic-net.

Ensembled GeneICL achieves the best average rank (4.64) across the 52 classification/regression tasks, e.g., AUROC 0.742, balanced accuracy 0.592, R2 0.274, ahead of TabFM (1.65B params), TabICLv2 (28M), TabPFN-3 (55.7M), and tuned elastic-net (rank 5.41).
With 4.24M parameters it uses up to 387x fewer than the strongest competitor (TabFM, 1.65B) and completes a cross-validation fold in 7.5 s with under 5 GB memory on a consumer laptop CPU.

For survival, the Cox-residual adaptation attains the highest aggregate C-index and best D-calibration across 28 SurvBoard cohorts (TCGA, ICGC, TARGET, METABRIC), within 0.001 of the best integrated Brier score, beating SurvPFN and other censoring adaptations.

Ablations show the prior matters more than architecture: swapping in the generic TabICLv2 prior drops regression R2 from 0.271 to 0.238 (real ARCHS4 profiles: 0.248), while untied 8-block versions (19.25M params) and full attention add cost without improving any metric.
summary.why: For anyone building AI for transcriptomics and multiomics, this is direct evidence that the pretraining objective and covariate prior — not model scale — are what currently limit clinical prediction from expression data, echoing prior reports that transcriptomic FMs underperform linear baselines. It also contributes a reusable 80-task translational benchmark and a tiny, CPU-deployable, per-cohort in-context model that sidesteps fine-tuning entirely.
summary.limitations: Results are limited to bulk RNA-seq (no single-cell or other omics), and each task is evaluated within a single cohort, leaving robustness to batch and platform shifts untested. Margins over tuned elastic-net are modest, and the authors leave open whether this reflects a ceiling of tens-to-hundreds of samples or of current priors.

also.title: GenoME: a MoE-based generative model for individualized, multimodal prediction and perturbation of genomic profiles.
also.abstract: The non-coding genome operates through a complex, multiscale regulatory system where regulated gene expressions are closely associated with cell-type-specific histone modifications, transcription factor binding, and 3D conformation. Developing computational models that can integrate these patterns to predict and interpret the regulatory system remains challenging. Here, we present GenoME, a Mixture of Experts (MoE)-based generative model that uses DNA sequence and cell-type-specific ATAC-seq signals to predict a unified genomic profiles encompassing epigenomics, transcriptomics, and chromatin architecture at base-pair to kilobase resolutions. GenoME enables multiscale predictions for held-out genomic regions and, critically, generalizes to predict the full regulatory landscape of unseen or individualized cell types from a single ATAC-seq input. We equip GenoME with an in silico perturbation framework that accurately forecasts the multimodal consequences of genetic perturbations and identifies functional enhancer-promoter connections, outperforming specialized models like Activity-by-Contact. These predictions can also be used to decipher the transcription factor grammar of cell-type-specific enhancers. GenoME thus provides a versatile, all-in-one platform for generative modeling, cross-cell-type generalization, and causal mechanistic investigation of the multiscale regulatory genome.

summary.tldr: GenoME is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) generative model that takes 1 Mb of DNA sequence plus a cell-type ATAC-seq track and jointly predicts RNA-seq (1-bp), splice junctions, CTCF and six histone ChIP-seq tracks (128-bp), and Hi-C contact maps, generalizing to unseen cell types without retraining.
summary.background: Sequence-only foundation models like Enformer, Borzoi, and AlphaGenome can only output tissue-averaged profiles because they cannot be conditioned on a specific cellular state. Existing cell-type-conditioned models (Enformer-Celltyping, EPCOT, GET, C.Origami) are single-modality, so unifying expression, epigenomics, and 3D conformation in one conditioned model remained unsolved.
summary.approach: GenoME encodes 1-Mb one-hot sequence plus ATAC signal with 1D-CNNs, then five Swin-Transformer-Mamba blocks with MoE feedforward layers (1 shared + 5 specialist experts, top-2 routing); U-Net-style decoders produce 1-bp RNA-seq and 128-bp ChIP tracks, and a 2D-CNN produces 512x512 Hi-C maps, with decoder MoE heads (1 shared + 8 experts) also gated by a context vector built from accessibility around 1216 PanglaoDB marker genes. It was trained on ENCODE data (89 ATAC groups: 63 tissues, 9 primary cells, 17 cell lines), with 2 RNA-seq, 7 ChIP-seq, and 1 Hi-C track per sample, on 8 A100 80GB GPUs (~80 h per task, batch 8-16, 100 epochs), holding out chr10/chr15. Three variants were trained: GenoME-basic (8 tissues), GenoME-ft (pretrained on 73 groups then finetuned), and GenoME-HCT116 (15 wild-type and genetically perturbed samples).
findings: On held-out chromosomes, GenoME matched or beat AlphaGenome on RNA-seq and H3K27ac prediction and outperformed Orca and C.Origami on Hi-C distance-stratified and insulation correlations; only HiCGen won on contacts beyond 0.7 Mb.
With no fine-tuning, de novo predictions for unseen liver and esophagus donors beat Enformer-Celltyping and EPCOT2, and Hi-C prediction for the unseen HCT116 line beat C.Origami and HiCGen.

In silico perturbations reproduced auxin-degradation experiments (CTCF, RAD21, CDK7, POLR2A), including H3K27me3 spreading over hundreds of kb after CTCF loss and transcriptional upregulation from the unseen CDK7 degradation.

A 'Grad-ABC' score (integrated gradients x predicted ABC) gave the best auPRC over ABC, ISM, and DeepLIFT for classifying 38 functional enhancers among 173 CRISPRi-FlowFISH E-P pairs in HCT116, transferring to K562.
For FAM3C, predicted perturbation effects correlated with measured CRISPRi expression changes (Pearson r = 0.53); a GET comparator reached 0.78 Pearson on fetal astrocytes.
summary.why: For multiomics model builders, GenoME demonstrates that conditioning a generative architecture on a cheap, widely available modality (ATAC-seq) plus MoE routing enables one model to cover expression, epigenomics, splicing, and conformation across arbitrary cell types. Its perturbation framework and Grad-ABC scoring provide a practical benchmark path against CRISPRi gold standards for enhancer-gene prioritization.
summary.limitations: Performance depends on high-quality deeply sequenced ATAC-seq (>=50M reads) and ENCODE-style tissue coverage, so very divergent cell states may degrade; also, HiCGen retains an edge for long-range contacts beyond the 1-Mb input window, and most headline correlations appear only in figures and supplements.
